idiom_name: Razor component owning state in @code; children take [Parameter] values / @bind
implementation_notes: A Razor component is an ordinary C# class: the state lives in the @code block (or a partial class), and child components are separate .razor files that receive data through [Parameter] properties and report changes through EventCallback or @bind - so a child can be rendered from literal parameters in a test or a design-time harness. Keep data access in the parent component, or in an injected service the parent wraps, and keep the children to markup plus parameters; the container is also where the interactive render mode boundary sits. Use this variant for Blazor applications, the MVVM variant for XAML stacks.
pitfalls: Copying a parameter into a field in the constructor or a one-shot initialization freezes the child on its first value; new parameter values arrive through the parameter-set lifecycle, so derive from the parameter instead of caching it.
Loading or computing in the render path repeats the work on every re-render; the container should load once and hand the immutable result down.
Mutating a collection outside Blazor's event path without a state-change signal leaves the UI stale, and children that mutate a collection they received as a parameter destroy the one-way flow.

variants.name: MVVM: viewmodel as container, XAML view bound to it
variants.idiom_name: INotifyPropertyChanged viewmodel + XAML view with {Binding} / BindingContext inheritance
variants.implementation_notes: In WPF, WinUI and .NET MAUI the container role belongs to a viewmodel: it holds the state, exposes it as properties that raise PropertyChanged (and as observable collections), and offers commands, while the view is a declarative document of bindings with no logic of its own. A binding context set on a parent is inherited by its children, which is literally the pattern's shape - state in the wrapper, children render what they are handed. Keep framework-aware work (dispatcher, dialogs, navigation) out of the viewmodel so it stays unit-testable.
pitfalls: Binding to a plain field or to a property without PropertyChanged produces a view that never updates; guard mutually updating properties with a change check or they ping-pong.
Viewmodels that hold Context, Dispatcher or control references leak UI concerns into the container and cannot be tested headlessly.
Two-way bindings with converters can hide a missing source of truth - if the view starts writing state the container never learns about, the separation is gone.
